title: Modules and Packages: Organizing Code Across Files
description: How Python modules/packages, Java packages, and C headers/source files compare for organizing multi-file code.

content.heading: Python
content.body: Any .py file is a module, importable with import module or from module import name. A package is a directory containing an __init__.py. There's no compile-time linking step — imports are resolved at runtime, by searching sys.path. pip and virtual environments manage third-party dependencies.

content.heading: Java
content.body: A package groups classes under a namespace (package com.example;), with the directory structure required to match the package name. import brings another package's classes into scope. Unlike Python, this is resolved at compile time (and again at class-loading time by the JVM), with the classpath determining where compiled classes/jars are found. Build tools (Maven, Gradle) manage dependencies, roughly analogous to pip.

content.heading: C
content.body: There's no module/package concept at the language level at all — organization is achieved purely by convention: a header file (.h) declares a module's public interface (function prototypes, type definitions), and a corresponding source file (.c) provides the implementation. #include textually pastes a header's contents in; the actual cross-file connections are resolved later, at link time, by the linker (not at compile time, and not via any language-level 'import' mechanism). There's no standard package manager built into the language, though various third-party tools (vcpkg, Conan) fill that role.

content.heading: Key Differences
content.body: Python's and Java's module/package systems are genuine language features, with defined namespacing, import resolution, and (for Java) compile-time checking; C's equivalent is a convention built on top of the preprocessor (#include) and the separate linking step, with no language-enforced namespacing at all (two unrelated global functions with the same name in different files is a link-time conflict, not something the language itself prevents earlier).

content.heading: When It Matters
content.body: Large C codebases rely heavily on naming conventions (prefixing function names by module, like mylib_init()) to avoid the naming collisions that Python's and Java's real namespacing prevents automatically.

keyPoints: Python's import/package system and Java's package system are genuine, namespaced language features
C has no module/package concept — headers (.h) plus source files (.c), connected via #include and the linker, is purely a convention
Only Java performs true compile-time namespace/import checking among the three
